summary: Defines Robust Header Compression (ROHC) profiles for compressing RTP/UDP-Lite/IP and UDP-Lite/IP packets, based on their differences from the profiles for UDP.

plainLanguage.summary: ROHC is a framework for shrinking the headers on packets that carry little data, such as voice calls. UDP-Lite needs profiles of its own because one of its header fields works differently from the UDP field it replaced. This RFC defines those profiles and the packet type that tells the receiver when the rules have changed.

questions: how does rohc compress udp-lite headers
what is the checksum coverage field
subtitle: Compressing UDP-Lite headers, whose checksum-coverage field does not behave like the UDP length field it replaced.

tldr.problem: UDP-Lite replaces the UDP length field with a checksum-coverage field, so the existing ROHC profiles for UDP cannot be reused unchanged.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two ROHC profiles, 0x0007 for RTP/UDP-Lite and 0x0008 for UDP-Lite, that classify the coverage field as inferred, static or changing, and add a CCE packet type that signals when the decompressor must start receiving the field again.
tldr.outcome: UDP-Lite headers compress as well as UDP headers when the coverage field behaves like a length field, and the two profile identifiers were registered with IANA.

facts.label: CCE packet type bits
facts.value: F and K in the packet type octet

today: RFC 4019 is a Proposed Standard and was later corrected by RFC 4815, which fixes and clarifies parts of RFC 3095 and applies to these profiles. The two profile identifiers 0x0007 and 0x0008 remain the registered names for RTP/UDP-Lite and UDP-Lite compression, and the profiles build on the framework in RFC 3095.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The ROHC working group built a header compression framework on top of which different profiles can be defined for different protocol sets or compression strategies. Because the cellular industry wanted an efficient way to carry voice over IP over wireless, ROHC focused on IP, UDP and RTP headers, which are generous in size compared with the payloads they often carry. ROHC RTP has become a very efficient, robust and capable compression scheme, able to compress headers down to a total size of one octet only, and it guarantees transparency to a very high extent even when residual bit errors are present in compressed headers delivered to the decompressor.

UDP-Lite is a transport protocol similar to UDP. It suits applications designed with the capability to tolerate errors in the payload, for which receiving damaged data is better than dealing with the loss of entire packets. That makes it a good fit for link technologies where data can be partially damaged, such as wireless links.

Although the two transport protocols are very similar, ROHC profiles must be defined separately for UDP-Lite headers because UDP-Lite does not share the same protocol identifier with UDP, and because the UDP-Lite checksum coverage field does not share the semantics of the corresponding UDP length field. It therefore cannot always be inferred. This document defines two ROHC profiles for efficient compression of UDP-Lite headers, whose objective is to provide simple modifications to the corresponding ROHC profiles for UDP specified in RFC 3095. The profiles also support some of the mechanisms defined in the ROHC IP-Only profile of RFC 3843: compression of multiple IP headers, compression of IP-ID fields with constant behaviour, improved mode transition logic, and a feedback option for decompressors with limited memory resources.
sections.plainLanguage: ROHC shrinks the headers on packets that carry little payload, such as voice. UDP-Lite needs its own profiles because one of its header fields works differently from the UDP field it replaced. This RFC defines two profiles that build on the existing UDP profiles with small changes.

sections.title: How UDP-Lite Differs from UDP
sections.content:
UDP-Lite is defined as an independent variant of the UDP transport protocol. It is very similar to UDP and lets applications that can tolerate errors in the payload use a checksum with an optional partial coverage. This is particularly useful with IPv6, where the use of the transport-layer checksum is mandatory.

UDP-Lite replaces the length field of the UDP header with a checksum coverage field. That field gives the number of octets covered by the 16-bit checksum, applied on a per-packet basis. The coverage area always includes the UDP-Lite header and may cover the entire packet, in which case UDP-Lite becomes semantically identical to UDP.

The RFC summarises the relationship in four points: UDP-Lite and UDP have different protocol identifiers; the UDP-Lite checksum cannot be disabled for IPv4; UDP-Lite redefines the UDP length field as the checksum coverage field, with different semantics; and UDP-Lite is semantically equivalent to UDP when the checksum coverage field indicates the total length of the packet.

The checksum itself is an end-to-end mechanism against erroneous delivery of error-sensitive data, and it is mandatory with IPv6 for both protocols. Unlike its UDP counterpart, the UDP-Lite checksum may not be transmitted as all zeroes and cannot be disabled for IPv4. For UDP, if the checksum is disabled the checksum field maintains a constant value and is normally not sent by the header compression scheme. If the UDP checksum is enabled, such an unpredictable field cannot be compressed and is sent uncompressed. The UDP length field, by contrast, is always redundant and can be provided by the IP module, so header compression schemes normally transmit no bits for it.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP-Lite works like UDP but can check only part of each packet. Instead of a length field it carries a checksum-coverage field that says how many bytes the checksum protects. Because that field has different rules, the compression scheme has to treat it separately.

sections.title: Three Change Patterns for the Coverage Field
sections.content:
The checksum coverage value is applied independently of other packets that may belong to the same flow. A single UDP-Lite packet is either entirely covered by the checksum, or covered up to some boundary that is less than the packet size but still includes the UDP-Lite header.

Across a sequence of packets, the value of the checksum coverage field may follow one of three change patterns. It may be changing while covering the entire packet. It may be unchanging, covering up to a fixed boundary within the packet. Or it may be changing without following any specific pattern.

The first pattern corresponds to the semantics of UDP when the UDP checksum is enabled. In that case the checksum coverage field varies according to the packet length and may be inferred from the IP header, just as the UDP length field value is. The second pattern is the case where the coverage is the same from one packet to another within a particular sequence, so the checksum coverage field may be a static value defined in the context and does not have to be sent in the compressed header. In the third case no useful change pattern can be identified, so the value must be sent along with every packet.

Any one of the patterns may predominate at any time during the lifetime of a flow. A flow that predominantly follows the first two patterns may provide opportunities for compressing the checksum coverage field for most of the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The coverage field can change in three ways from packet to packet: it changes while always covering the whole packet, it stays the same, or it changes unpredictably. Each pattern leads to a different compression rule, and a flow may switch between them over its lifetime.

sections.title: Why a Separate Profile Is Needed
sections.content:
Simplicity is a strong motivation for the design of the UDP-Lite header compression profiles. They should entail only a few simple modifications to the corresponding profiles defined for UDP in RFC 3095, and it is desirable to include some of the improvements found in the ROHC IP-Only profile. Whenever UDP-Lite is used in a manner that is semantically identical to UDP, the compression efficiency should be similar.

The simplest approach would be to treat the checksum coverage field as an irregular value and send it uncompressed for every packet, which can be achieved by adding the field to the definition of the general packet format. The compression efficiency would then always be less than for UDP.

Some care is needed to achieve a compression efficiency for UDP-Lite similar to that of UDP when the checksum coverage field behaves like the UDP length field. That requires the possibility to infer the checksum coverage field when it is equal to the length of the packet. Without it, UDP-Lite would be at a disadvantage over links where header compression is used, when its behaviour is made similar to the semantics of UDP. A mechanism to detect the presence of the checksum coverage field in compressed headers is therefore needed, and this is achieved by defining a new packet type with the identifiers left unused in RFC 3095.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending the coverage field in every packet would be simple but wasteful. To keep UDP-Lite as cheap to send as UDP, the profiles let the receiver work out the field when it equals the packet length, and add a special packet type for signalling when that assumption no longer holds.

sections.title: Context Parameters That Drive Compression
sections.content:
Information about previous packets is maintained in a context, including information describing the packet stream and the compression parameters. Although UDP and UDP-Lite share many commonalities, one parameter from RFC 3095 does not apply: the parameter context(UDP Checksum), because the UDP-Lite checksum cannot be disabled as opposed to UDP.

The UDP-Lite checksum is always sent as-is in every compressed packet, but the checksum coverage field may not always be sent in each compressed packet. The parameter context(CFP), the Coverage Field Present flag, controls this. If it is nonzero, the checksum coverage field is not compressed and is present within compressed packets. If it is zero, the field is compressed and is not sent. That is the case when the value follows a stable inter-packet change pattern, either a constant value or a value equal to the packet length for most packets in a sequence.

The parameter context(CFI), the Coverage Field Inferred flag, says whether the field should be inferred or taken from a value previously saved in the context. If it is nonzero, the checksum coverage field is inferred from the packet length, similarly to the UDP length field in ROHC RTP. If it is zero, the field is decompressed using context(UDP-Lite Checksum Coverage). When context(CFI) is updated to a nonzero value, the value of the checksum coverage field stored in the context must also be updated.

The RFC fixes the initial values. During context initialisation, context(CFP) must be set to a nonzero value if the checksum coverage field differs from the length of the UDP-Lite packet in any IR or IR-DYN packet sent or received, and to zero otherwise. context(CFI) must be set to a nonzero value if the checksum coverage field equals the packet length within an IR or an IR-DYN packet, and to zero otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor and the decompressor keep a shared memory of the flow, called a context. Two flags in it decide whether the coverage field travels in every packet or is worked out from the packet length instead.

sections.title: Packet Formats and Recovery Logic
sections.content:
The general packet format of a compressed ROHC UDP-Lite header is similar to the compressed ROHC RTP header of RFC 3095, with modifications to the checksum field and additional fields for handling multiple IP headers and for the UDP-Lite checksum coverage. A list of dynamic header chains carries the dynamic header part for each IP header in excess of the initial two. The UDP-Lite checksum coverage field takes two octets if context(CFP) equals 1 or the packet type is CCE, and the UDP-Lite checksum always takes two octets. The order of the fields following the optional extension of the general ROHC packet format is the same as the order between the fields in the uncompressed header, and the checksum coverage field is CRC-DYNAMIC when the CRC is calculated.

The profiles define a packet type called Checksum Coverage Extension, or CCE, whose updating properties depend on the final two bits, F and K, of the packet type octet. The value 00 is reserved at framework level, 01 indicates CCE(), 10 indicates CCE(ON) and 11 indicates CCE(OFF). The two-octet checksum coverage field is always present in this packet format.

CCE() changes no context value other than those of the inner packet type it carries, so it can extend any of the packet types 2, 1 and 0 regardless of the current mode of operation. It is useful when the checksum coverage deviates from the change pattern the compressor assumed, and the deviations are rare. CCE(ON) updates context(CFP) to a nonzero value, which effectively turns on the presence of the checksum coverage field in the general packet format; this is useful when the predominant change pattern precludes its compression. CCE(OFF) updates context(CFP) to zero, updates context(CFI) to a nonzero value if the field equals the packet length and to zero otherwise, and also updates context(UDP-Lite Checksum Coverage). Neither CCE(ON) nor CCE(OFF) may be used to extend R-0 and R-1* headers.

The compressor logic says that when the checksum coverage field differs from the stored context value, and differs from the packet length while context(CFP) is zero, the field cannot be compressed and must be sent uncompressed using a CCE packet, or the context must be reinitialised with an IR packet. On the decompressor side, for packet types other than IR, IR-DYN and CCE received when context(CFP) is zero, the field is decompressed from the value stored in the context if context(CFI) is zero, and otherwise it is inferred from the length of the UDP-Lite packet derived from the IP module.

Two further mechanisms come from the ROHC IP-Only profile. The mode parameter value 0 in the UOR-2, IR and IR-DYN packet types is redefined as cancel mode transition, so that the compressor can decline a mode transition requested by the decompressor; on receiving it the decompressor must stay in its current mode and should refrain from sending further requests for the declined mode. The CONTEXT_MEMORY feedback option, with option type 9 and option length 0, tells the compressor that the decompressor does not have enough memory for the context the current compressed structure requires, and the compressor should then compress the stream in a way that needs less decompressor memory or stop compressing it.
sections.plainLanguage: When the coverage field stops following the assumed pattern, the compressor sends a CCE packet. It either tells the decompressor to start sending the field again, or to work it out from the packet length. If the field cannot be compressed at all, the compressor restarts the context with an IR packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states in one sentence that the security considerations of RFC 3095 apply integrally to this document, without modification. It adds no security rules of its own, because the profiles only change how a header field is carried, not how the protected payload is handled.

The framework itself notes that ROHC is designed to be robust: transparency is guaranteed to an extremely high extent even when residual bit errors are present in compressed headers delivered to the decompressor.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds no security rules of its own. It says that the security considerations of the ROHC framework apply here unchanged, and the framework is designed to recover from bit errors in compressed headers.

sections.title: Profile Identifiers Registered with IANA
sections.content:
Two ROHC profile identifiers have been reserved by IANA for the profiles defined in this document: 0x0007 for ROHC RTP/UDP-Lite and 0x0008 for ROHC UDP-Lite. Profile number 0x0006 is being saved for the TCP/IP profile, so 0x0007 and 0x0008 are the most suitable unused identifiers available. As for previous ROHC profiles, the numbers 0xnn07 and 0xnn08 must also be reserved for future variants of these profiles.

The registration for the RObust Header Compression profile identifiers name space keeps the range 0x0006 to 0xnn7F as to be assigned by IANA, with 0xnn06 also to be assigned, 0x0007 marked as ROHC RTP/UDP-Lite with 0xnn07 reserved, 0x0008 marked as ROHC UDP-Lite with 0xnn08 reserved, and 0x0009 to 0xnn7F to be assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA assigned two numbers for these profiles: one for RTP over UDP-Lite and one for plain UDP-Lite. Numbers of the same shape are held back for future versions of the same profiles.

fields.name: Checksum Coverage
fields.desc: Number of octets covered by the 16-bit checksum. Always includes the header.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: The 16-bit checksum. May not be disabled and is never sent as all zeroes.

viz.caption: THE THREE CHANGE PATTERNS OF THE COVERAGE FIELD

items.title: Pattern 1: changing, whole packet covered
items.text: Matches UDP with an enabled checksum. The coverage field follows the packet length, so it is INFERRED.

items.title: Pattern 2: unchanging, fixed boundary
items.text: The coverage field keeps the same value across the sequence, so it is STATIC and stays in the context.

items.title: Pattern 3: changing with no pattern
items.text: No useful change pattern can be found, so the field is CHANGING and is sent with every packet.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Reserved at framework level for IR-DYN.

items.label: CCE()
items.desc: Carries the coverage field and updates no context value of its own.

items.label: CCE(ON)
items.desc: Turns on the presence of the checksum coverage field in compressed packets.

items.label: CCE(OFF)
items.desc: Turns the field off and updates the inferred flag and the stored coverage value.
